data.content_ref: inline:The claim grounds the preference for better-corroborated theories in two features: (1) higher empirical content and (2) having survived severe tests, concluding this makes the theory 'the best available target for future criticism.' But empirical content is a synchronic logical property of a theory (what it rules out), independent of its testing history. Therefore 'survived severe tests' must be doing load-bearing work distinct from content—otherwise 'better-corroborated' collapses into merely 'higher-content and not-yet-falsified,' and corroboration (severity of tests passed) adds nothing. Yet the claim provides no non-inductive justification for why past test-survival makes a theory a better *future* target for criticism. If past survival provides zero information about future prospects (as the claim insists by denying any inductive link), then a high-content unfalsified theory that has never been tested is an equally good target for future criticism as one that has survived many severe tests. The only way past survival becomes relevant to future critical practice is if one assumes that a theory's track record carries forward some weight in its future candidacy—which is precisely the inductive assumption the claim disowns. The claim thus faces a dilemma: either corroboration (test history) is irrelevant to the preference—making Popper's actual emphasis on severe tests unmotivated—or it is relevant, which requires induction. The target's own countercondition flags exactly this vulnerability ('If one can demonstrate that acting on the best-corroborated theory logically entails an assumption that the future will resemble the past (induction), then the preference is indefensible on Popperian terms'), and the claim's defense fails to escape it because 'best target for future criticism' is itself a forward-looking evaluative judgment that cannot be grounded in past survival without induction.
